html:
The general election held in South Africa from 26 to 29 April 1994, the first in which people of every race could vote. It ended apartheid, the system of racial rule in place since 1948.

The road to it began in 1990, when Nelson Mandela walked out of prison after 27 years. Talks between his African National Congress (ANC) and the government of F. W. de Klerk produced an interim constitution, through years of violence that many feared would wreck the vote. Millions queued for hours, many voting for the first time in their lives, and almost 20 million votes were counted.

The ANC won 62 percent. The new National Assembly elected Mandela president, the country's first black head of state. He led a Government of National Unity with De Klerk's National Party and the Inkatha Freedom Party. Since then 27 April has been Freedom Day. Two years later the Truth and Reconciliation Commission began hearing what apartheid had done. In the same month as the vote, the genocide in Rwanda began, a grim contrast across the continent.
sum: The general election held in South Africa from 26 to 29 April 1994, the first in which people of every race could vote. It ended apartheid, the system of racial rule in place since 1948.
